manifest.name: comms-adherence-gate
manifest.description: Judges every Slack-facing store-progress completion and agent Slack post against the comms preferences of the requester, or of the person it @-mentions, their latest request and a plain-language rubric with Jev (TypeSafe or OpenRouter), and in enforce blocks a failing call once per task

comms-adherence-gate.readme:
# comms-adherence-gate

Agents finish Slack tasks with a final message a human reads, and post to Slack threads directly. This extension judges that text with Jev, [TypeSafe](https://typesafe.ai)'s decision model: against the requester's stated comms preferences and their latest request, and against a plain-language rubric that applies to every message. In `enforce` it blocks a failing call once and tells the agent what to fix. A `plain` failure points the agent at the `comms` skill.

Install config:

```json
{ "mode": "shadow", "plainMode": "shadow" }
```

Start in `shadow`, read the verdicts in KV for a few days, then switch to `enforce`. `mode` and `plainMode` move independently.

## Modes

| `mode` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `off` | Never evaluates. |
| `shadow` (default) | Asks Jev and records the verdict. Never blocks. |
| `enforce` | Asks Jev, records the verdict, and blocks the call when a dimension fails, at most `maxBlocksPerTask` times per task. The agent gets the failed dimensions, their scores and the stated preference, and calls again. |

`mode` governs the preference dimensions (`verbosity`, `tone`, `language`). `plainMode` governs `plain`. A dimension blocks only when its own mode is `enforce`. Both share one block budget per task, across every gated tool.

## What it gates

Hook: `pre.tool.call` on:

- `store-progress` with `status: "completed"` and a non-empty `output`, on a task that came from Slack (`source = "slack"` or a `slackThreadTs`). Other completions pass without a Jev call.
- `slack-reply`, `slack-post`, `slack-start-thread` and `slack-update`, judged on `message`. The task is `slack-reply`'s `taskId`, else the caller's task context. A post with no task context passes.

Only a call the tool itself accepts is judged, so no other task's text reaches Jev. For `store-progress` the caller must own the task, the task must be unassigned, or the caller must be a lead. For the Slack tools the caller must be the task's assignee or its creator, the rule `slack-reply` enforces. Calls made by extensions are skipped. Script SDK calls never reach `pre.tool.call` (the tool registrar dispatches it only for MCP calls); if one ever does, the gate records it and never blocks.

A requester with no stated preferences in `users.metadata.comms` still gets the `plain` question. Set preferences with the `manage-user` tool.

In a thread with several people, the requester is the person whose message created the task. A message that @-mentions someone (`<@U123>`) is judged against the first mentioned person with stored preferences, resolved through their Slack identity in `user_external_ids`; otherwise against the requester. The lookup is one SQL read, only when the text mentions someone and `mode` is not `off`. The verdict records who was judged in `judgedFor` (`mention` or `requester`) and `audience`.

## Decision

The gate reads the task row and asks one `noul` question per stated preference it knows: `verbosity`, `tone`, `language`. Any other key in `comms` is context only.

Jev sees the preferences, the requester's latest message (the text after the last `</thread_context>`, from the last 1,400 characters of the task), the first 400 characters of the task, and the output. Its judging rules say an explicit request outranks the stored default. A requested long answer, story or document is not a verbosity failure.

It also asks `plain` on every message unless `plainMode` is `off` or the text is a JSON document (structured output for an `outputSchema`). The rubric comes from the `comms` skill: everyday words, one idea per sentence, every number with a unit and a direction word, and no unexplained shorthand (n, median, p90, cohort, baseline, delta, `±X at 95%`). Code identifiers, task ids, PR numbers, links and versions are fine. Jev gets contrasting plain and dense examples in `plain_language_rules`; a prose-only rubric scored plain rewrites as low as the dense originals.

All questions go in one Jev request. A preference dimension fails below `threshold`; `plain` fails below `plainThreshold`. Any failed dimension fails the message.

### Calibration of `plain`

Jev scores dense status text near 0 and plain text near 0.8 to 0.9, with a wide middle of compact but readable engineering notes. Measured on 400 Slack-facing completions over 7 days, at `threshold` 0.75 for preferences:

| `plainThreshold` | Newly blocked (of messages that pass today) |
|---|---|
| 0.75 | 81% to 83% |
| 0.3 | 9% to 13% |
| 0.25 (default) | 5% to 7% |

At 0.25 the dense prompt-cache-monitor post scores about 0.15 and its plain rewrite about 0.81.

## Jev transport

Jev is reachable two ways. Both take the same request and return the same answer.

| `provider` | Endpoint | Key | Model |
|---|---|---|---|
| `typesafe` | `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` (or `apiKey`) | `model`, default `jev-latest` |
| `openrouter` | `POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | `openrouterModel`, default `typesafe/jev-1.13` |
| `auto` (default) | TypeSafe when its key is set, else OpenRouter | | |

Each verdict row records the `provider` that answered.

## Fail open

Every error lets the completion through: a missing key, an HTTP error, a network error, a timeout, a malformed answer, or a failed DB read. The handler never throws, so an outage cannot auto-disable the extension. Each failure bumps the `error` counter and overwrites `error:last`.

## Self-test

Call `store-progress` with a non-completed status and `progress` starting with `comms-gate-selftest`. The gate judges a known-bad and a known-good message against a terse preference, and a dense and a plain message on `plain`, then writes `selftest:last`: every score, both thresholds, the provider, `controlsOk` (verbosity: bad below `threshold`, good at or above it) and `plainControlsOk` (the same against `plainThreshold`). Real traffic is untouched.

## Config

| Key | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `shadow` | `off`, `shadow`, or `enforce` |
| `threshold` | `0.5` | A preference dimension scoring below this fails |
| `plainMode` | `shadow` | `off`, `shadow`, or `enforce` for the `plain` dimension |
| `plainThreshold` | `0.25` | `plain` scoring below this fails. See [Calibration](#calibration-of-plain) |
| `timeoutMs` | `4000` | Jev call timeout, capped at 4000 (the dispatcher cancels a handler at 5 s) |
| `maxBlocksPerTask` | `1` | Blocks per task in `enforce`; after that the gate records and lets it through |
| `provider` | `auto` | `auto`, `typesafe`, or `openrouter`. See [Jev transport](#jev-transport) |
| `model` | `jev-latest` | Jev model on TypeSafe |
| `openrouterModel` | `typesafe/jev-1.13` | Jev model on OpenRouter |
| `apiKey` | unset | Explicit TypeSafe key. Prefer the `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` secret below |

## Required secrets

Read from the API process environment at call time. Set them as global `swarm_config` secrets: the API process loads global rows into `process.env` at boot and on config reload.

- `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`: one is required for any evaluation. Under `auto`, TypeSafe wins when both are set. Without either, every completion fails open.

No key is written to config, KV, logs, or a block reason.

## KV namespace `ext:comms-gate`

- `last`: the latest verdict, with `tool`, `scores`, `failed`, `mode`, `plainMode`, `provider`, `latencyMs`, the preferences, a 400-character `askPreview` and a 700-character `outputPreview`.
- `fail:<epochMs>:<taskId>`: one row per failed verdict, with `action` (`blocked` or `recorded`).
- `blocks:<taskId>`: blocks issued for that task.
- `error:last`, `selftest:last`.
- Counters: `total`, `pass`, `fail`, `blocked`, `escaped` (a blocking dimension failed, block budget spent), `shadowed` (only non-blocking dimensions failed), `error`, and `dim:<dimension>`.

## Known limits

- Only the last 1,400 characters of the task are searched for the latest request. A very long final message is cut to its last 900 characters.
- The block budget is per task, so a retried call after a block goes through once the budget is spent, even if it still fails.
- Each gated Slack post waits for one Jev call (about 0.2 s measured, capped by `timeoutMs`).

manifest.name: deploy-awareness
manifest.description: Appends a one-line note to new tasks while a Dokploy compose deploy is in progress

deploy-awareness.readme:
# deploy-awareness

Appends one line to a new task's description while a Dokploy compose deploy is in progress, so the worker knows it may restart soon:

```
Note: a prod deploy started at 14:05 UTC is in progress; your worker may restart in the next few minutes. Checkpoint with store-progress before long steps.
```

Install config:

```json
{ "composeId": "<compose id>" }
```

Optional keys: `label` (the environment word in the note, default `prod`), `cacheTtlMs` (how long a check result, a failure included, is reused, default 120000), `timeoutMs` (caps the Dokploy call, default 2000), `staleAfterMs` (a deployment still `running` after this long is a stuck record and is ignored, default 1800000).

The Dokploy API key and URL are not extension config. Config is writable by a lead, and a key name or a host there would let it point the API process at any env secret and any host. They come from the API process environment:

- `DOKPLOY_API_KEY`: required. A global `swarm_config` secret. The API process loads global rows into `process.env` at boot and on config reload. `ctx.swarm.config_get` cannot serve this, because the SDK scrubs every response and a secret comes back as `[REDACTED:<name>]`.
- `DOKPLOY_BASE_URL`: optional, default `https://app.dokploy.com`. It must be an `https` URL. Anything else, including an unparseable value, sends no request and logs a warning that names the variable and not its value.

The key is never written to config, state, logs, or a description.

How it decides: it calls `GET /api/deployment.allByCompose?composeId=...`, takes the deployment with the newest `createdAt`, and counts a deploy as in progress when that deployment's `status` is `running`. Dokploy statuses are `running`, `done`, `error`, and `cancelled`.

Fail open: a missing key, a non-https `DOKPLOY_BASE_URL`, a Dokploy error, a bad response, or a timeout adds no line, and the task is created as usual. The handler never throws, so an outage cannot auto-disable the extension. A task whose description already carries the note (a resume or a follow-up) is left alone.

At most one Dokploy call runs per `cacheTtlMs` window. The cache lives in `ctx.state`, so API replicas share it, and tasks created at the same moment share one in-flight check.

manifest.name: github-sender-allowlist
manifest.description: Blocks GitHub webhook tasks from senders outside configured allowlists

github-sender-allowlist.readme:
# github-sender-allowlist

Blocks GitHub webhook tasks from senders outside the configured allowlists. Login matching is case-insensitive. Tasks from other sources pass through. No task type is exempt by default.

Config:

```json
{
  "internal": ["tarasyarema", "harlequinetcie"],
  "external": ["fuvidani", "capchase-bot"],
  "reviewBots": [],
  "exemptTaskTypes": []
}
```

Internal senders can create any GitHub task, including reviews. Logins in `reviewBots` can create `github-review` tasks only. External senders can create `github-comment` or `github-pr` tasks on pull requests, and `github-review` tasks when `vcsUrl` contains `/pull/`. Choose any review-bot logins from the sender census in the [security audit](https://live.agent-fs.dev/file/~/648a5f3c-35c8-4f11-8673-b89de52cd6bd/2faf73ba-4eee-4472-8b3b-359c4ed6bfbb/thoughts/a09d19a4-bd35-4593-9b6f-c2ccafccead8/reviews/2026-09-28-github-sender-authorization-audit.md) when installing the extension; the template intentionally defaults to an empty list.

`exemptTaskTypes` is an optional operator override for explicitly exempting task types. It defaults to an empty list. The GitHub handler does not pass the action for `github-pr` tasks, so external `github-pr` access also permits assignment and label events on pull requests.

manifest.name: notify-on-complete
manifest.description: Posts a short summary to a Slack channel when a task completes or fails

notify-on-complete.readme:
# notify-on-complete

Posts one Slack message per finished task to a channel of your choice. Uses `ctx.swarm.slack_post`, so the message is sent by the swarm bot on behalf of the `ext:notify-on-complete` identity.

Config:

```json
{ "channelId": "C0123456789", "includeFailed": true, "maxOutputChars": 400 }
```

Post hooks run after the task change is committed and cannot block or modify anything. A Slack failure counts as a handler failure; five in a row auto-disable the extension.

manifest.name: require-ticket-ref
manifest.description: Blocks new tasks from selected origins unless the description names a ticket

require-ticket-ref.readme:
# require-ticket-ref

Blocks new tasks that do not name a ticket. Applies to the origins listed in `config.origins` (default `rest`, `mcp`, `slack`), so schedules, workflows, webhooks, and follow-ups keep working.

Config:

```json
{ "pattern": "\\bDES-\\d+\\b", "origins": ["rest", "mcp", "slack"] }
```

Effect: REST returns `422` with the reason, `send-task` returns an error result, and Slack replies with the reason in the thread. The extension state keeps a `blocked:<origin>` counter.

manifest.name: require-verification-note
manifest.description: Refuses task completion unless the output contains a verification line

require-verification-note.readme:
# require-verification-note

Guards `store-progress` with `status: "completed"`. The call is refused until the `output` contains the configured marker (default `Verified:`). The agent sees the reason as a tool error and can retry with a corrected output.

Config:

```json
{ "marker": "Verified:" }
```

The guard covers agent MCP calls only. REST and dashboard completions are not tool calls and pass through.

manifest.name: slack-reply-gate
manifest.description: Asks a SystemOne decision model (Jev or Clef) whether Lead should answer a buffered Slack thread follow-up, and drops the wake-up when it should not

slack-reply-gate.readme:
# slack-reply-gate

Lead is woken by every human message in a Slack thread the swarm takes part in, including "lol", an emoji, or two people chatting with each other. This extension asks a SystemOne decision model, Jev ([TypeSafe](https://typesafe.ai)) or Clef (Cloudflare Workers AI), whether Lead should answer a new thread message, and drops the wake-up when it should not.

Install config:

```json
{ "mode": "shadow" }
```

Start in `shadow`, read the decisions in KV for a few days, then switch to `enforce`.

## Modes

| `mode` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `off` | Never evaluates. |
| `shadow` (default) | Asks the model and records the verdict. Never blocks. |
| `enforce` | Asks the model, records the verdict, and blocks the Lead task when the answer is no. The message gets :mute: instead: no Lead task, no reply, no outcome card. |

## What it gates

Hook: `pre.task.create`, for tasks with origin `slack` whose description carries the thread buffer's header `[Thread follow-up — N message(s) buffered]`. Those are the non-mention thread replies that `src/slack/thread-buffer.ts` batches into a Lead task. A direct @mention of the bot creates a task without that header and is never gated.

The header counts only at the start of the description or right after the closing `</thread_context>`. Thread context quotes old messages verbatim, and an older Lead reply can quote the header itself, so a header inside the context is ignored. Only the text after the real header is treated as new.

## Decision

1. A follow-up with downloaded files (status `draft`) passes without a decision call.
2. **@mention pass-through.** A new message that @mentions Lead passes without a decision call. A mention is the bot mention the engine rewrites to `<@U…> (that's you)`, a resolved `<@U…|lead>`, or a literal `@lead` (any name in `leadAliases`). Only the new messages are scanned, never the thread context, so an old mention earlier in the thread does not pass later banter.
3. Otherwise one decision call (one `choice` question, see [Provider](#provider)) with the new message(s), the sender kind, and the last `contextMessages` thread messages. Labels: `direct_ask`, `followup_to_lead`, `instruction_to_lead`, `reaction_only`, `banter_between_others`, `not_addressed_to_lead`, `other`.
4. The answer is no only when the top label is `reaction_only`, `banter_between_others`, or `not_addressed_to_lead`, and the summed probability of those three labels is at least `minConfidence`. A split between two skip labels is still a skip. An unsure verdict replies.

Several buffered messages are judged together. One mention in any of them passes the batch.

## Provider

The decision is made on the API server by the `system-one-decide` tool (`ctx.swarm.systemOne_decide`), the same path a `system-one-decision` workflow node takes. The server reads the provider's credential, sends the request, and validates the answer, so every SystemOne host works and no key enters the hook.

| `provider` | Model | Credential |
|---|---|---|
| `typesafe` | Jev, `model` (default `jev-latest`) | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` |
| `openrouter` | Jev, `openrouterModel` (default `typesafe/jev-1.13`) | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| `cloudflare` | Clef, `cloudflareModel` (default `clef`, or `clef-flash`) | `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` (or `CLOUDFLARE_API_KEY`) and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` |
| `laya`, `openai` | The host's default model | See the workflows guide |
| `auto` (default) | The first of typesafe, openrouter, cloudflare whose credential is set. A provider the server refuses for a deployment setting (openrouter when `OPENROUTER_BASE_URL` points at a gateway) is skipped for the next one | |

With no credential for `auto`, every message fails open and the KV row names the secrets. Each decision row records the `provider` that answered. `minConfidence` was tuned on Jev; check Clef's verdicts in `shadow` before you enforce on it.

## Fail open

Every error lets the task through: a missing key, a provider error relayed by the server, a network error, a timeout, a malformed answer, or an unknown label. The handler never throws, so an outage cannot auto-disable the extension. Each failure is recorded as `fail-open` in KV and logged as a warning.

## :mute: on drop (enforce)

No swarm tool or extension `ctx` method adds a Slack reaction, so the hook calls the Slack Web API with the bot token. It needs the `reactions:write` scope, which the Slack app already uses for its acceptance reactions.

1. `reactions.remove` for each acceptance reaction the engine may have put on the triggering message: `eyes`, `heavy_plus_sign`, `zap`, `speech_balloon`, or their `SLACK_REACTION_ACCEPTED`, `SLACK_REACTION_BUFFERED`, `SLACK_REACTION_NOW`, and `SLACK_REACTION_STEERED` overrides. Slack only removes the bot's own reaction, so a human's :eyes: stays.
2. `reactions.add` with `muteReaction` (default `mute`). `already_reacted` counts as success. Skipped when `muteReaction` is `""`.

The block returns first and the Slack calls run after it. A slow or failing Slack call never delays the drop or turns it back into a task. Set `muteReaction` to `""` for a true no-op: step 1 still clears the bot's acceptance reaction(s), and nothing is added.

## Config

| Key | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `shadow` | `off`, `shadow`, or `enforce` |
| `timeoutMs` | `3000` | Decision call timeout, capped at 4000 (the dispatcher cancels a handler at 5 s) |
| `provider` | `auto` | `auto`, `typesafe`, `openrouter`, `cloudflare`, `laya`, or `openai`. See [Provider](#provider) |
| `model` | `jev-latest` | Jev model on TypeSafe |
| `openrouterModel` | `typesafe/jev-1.13` | Jev model on OpenRouter |
| `cloudflareModel` | `clef` | Clef model on Cloudflare Workers AI |
| `minConfidence` | `0.55` | Minimum summed skip probability to skip |
| `contextMessages` | `6` | Thread messages sent to the model, 0 to 20 |
| `leadAliases` | `["lead"]` | A literal `@alias` in a new message counts as a mention |
| `botSlackUserIds` | `[]` | Slack user ids labelled `bot` as the sender for the model |
| `muteReaction` | `mute` | Reaction for a dropped message; `""` only removes the acceptance reaction(s) |
| `slackTimeoutMs` | `5000` | Timeout per Slack call |

## Required secrets

Set them as global `swarm_config` values. The server reads the provider credential from the global row when it makes the decision. `auto` and the Slack token read the API process environment, which loads global rows at boot and on config reload.

- One provider credential from the [Provider](#provider) table is required for any evaluation. Without one, every message fails open. The `apiKey` config field of earlier versions is gone: the hook never holds a key, so store it as the global `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` secret.
- `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`: the Slack app's bot token. A swarm with Slack connected already has it. Without it, `enforce` still drops the message but cannot touch its reactions, and logs a `mute-error`.

No key is written to config, KV, logs, or a description.

## KV namespace `ext:slack-reply-gate`

- `d:<epochMs>:<channel>_<threadTs>`: one row per decision, with `action` (`pass`, `shadow-skip`, `skipped`, `fail-open`), `provider`, `reason`, `confidence`, `skipP`, `latencyMs`, `sender`, and a 300-character `preview`.
- `m:<epochMs>:<channel>_<threadTs>`: one row per mute attempt, with `action` (`muted`, `unreacted` when `muteReaction` is `""`, `mute-error`), `removed`, `added`, and `errors`.
- `last`: the latest decision. Mute rows never overwrite it.
- Counters: `total`, `mention`, `files`, `reply`, `shadow-skip`, `skipped`, `error`, `muted`, `unreacted`, `mute-error`, and `reason:<label>`.

## Known limits

- When Lead already has an active task in the thread, the buffer steers that task instead of creating one, so `pre.task.create` does not fire and the gate does not run.
- A blocked flush makes the thread buffer log a `TaskCreationBlockedError`. Nothing is lost: the next follow-up's `<thread_context>` carries the earlier messages.
- A flush of several messages mutes only the triggering (last) message. The others keep their acceptance reaction.

manifest.name: task-digest
manifest.description: Daily digest of tasks completed and failed in the last 24 hours

scripts.name: task-digest-collect
scripts.description: Count tasks completed and failed in the last 24 hours and summarize them
scripts.intent: Produce a daily digest of swarm task outcomes

schedules.name: task-digest-daily
schedules.description: Runs task-digest-collect every day at 09:00 UTC

files.workflows/report.yaml:
# A workflow file an extension ships. Its name must start with "task-digest-".
name: task-digest-report
description: Collect the task digest on demand. Trigger it manually.
definition:
  nodes:
    - id: collect
      type: swarm-script
      label: Collect the digest
      config:
        scriptName: task-digest-collect
        scope: global
        args:
          hours: 24
files.skills/task-digest-guide/SKILL.md:
---
name: task-digest-guide
description: Read the task-digest extension's output. Use when someone asks how many tasks completed or failed recently, or which agents did them.
---

# Reading the task digest

The `task-digest` extension ships a script, a schedule and a workflow that count recent task outcomes.

## Get a digest

- Run the script: `script-run name="task-digest-collect" scope="global" args={"hours": 24}`.
- Or trigger the `task-digest-report` workflow; its `collect` step output holds the same result.
- The `task-digest-daily` schedule runs the script every day at 09:00 UTC while the extension is enabled.

## Read the result

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `completed`, `failed` | Task counts in the window |
| `byAgent` | Per-agent `{completed, failed}`; `(unassigned)` for tasks with no agent |
| `since` | Start of the window (ISO time) |
| `summary` | One line you can paste into a reply |

A sample result is bundled as `files/example-output.json`.

Counts come from `task_list` with a limit of 500 per status, so a very busy window can undercount.

task-digest.readme:
# task-digest

Ships a script, a schedule, a workflow, and a skill alongside its hooks. It is the reference for extensions that bundle assets.

| Asset | Name | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Script | `task-digest-collect` | Counts tasks completed and failed in the last `hours` (default 24), grouped by agent |
| Schedule | `task-digest-daily` | Runs the script every day at 09:00 UTC with `{ "hours": 24 }` |
| Workflow | `task-digest-report` | One `swarm-script` node that runs the script with `{ "hours": 24 }`. It has no triggers, so you trigger it by hand. |
| Skill | `task-digest-guide` | Tells agents how to get and read a digest. Bundles `example-output.json`. |
| Hooks | `hooks.ts` | Counts `post.task.completed` and `post.task.failed` in the extension state |

Install creates every asset, owned by the `ext:task-digest` agent. The script is callable at once. The schedule, workflow, and skill stay off until the extension is enabled. Disabling the extension turns them off again.

```bash
bun scripts/extensions/install-template.ts task-digest --enable
```

Run the script by hand with `script-run name="task-digest-collect" scope="global" args={"hours":24}`.

Run the workflow with `trigger-workflow` after you enable the extension.

The skill is global, so no agent sees it yet. After you enable the extension, install it on each agent that needs it with `skill-install`.

No config.
